channel.title: Southern Watch
channel.description: A daily foreign and security brief from an Australian angle, with how Beijing, Moscow, Tehran and Pyongyang frame each story.

item.title: Iran threatens US bases in Europe, claims two more mined tankers; Bessent moves to a military base
item.description:
What happened

  • 11 Nov: Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, told Al Mayadeen that Iran "may target certain US military bases in Europe" if it is attacked again (as reported by Mehr). He said targets could include distant US installations and "certain islands", especially any used by aircraft that strike Iran. Iran would not limit itself to targets hit in earlier rounds.
  • Rezaei repeated that there are no direct talks with the US. Iran has put seven conditions and is waiting for a clear answer. He said no enriched nuclear material, not even a small amount, will leave Iran.
  • 11 Nov: The IRGC Navy said two more tankers hit mines while leaving the strait by an "unauthorized" route, with transponders off and under US air cover. It says both burned and were abandoned. No ship names or flags were given. This is unconfirmed. Maritime authorities have not verified the IRGC's recent mine-strike claims, and CENTCOM has said earlier in the war that no ships have hit mines in the strait.
  • Iran's strait authority said it took "legal action" against two bulk carriers using forged documents. Speaker Ghalibaf, via TASS, said Iran has an understanding with Oman on a shipping corridor and has had no official US reply to its conditions.
  • 10–11 Nov: The US Treasury confirmed that Secretary Scott Bessent and his family moved from their Washington home to a military base after Iranian threats (first reported by the New York Times). Bessent runs the sanctions campaign against Iran. Reuters saw a late-October intelligence memo warning that Iranian plots against Americans had reached an advanced stage. Iran denies plotting against US officials.
  • Oil: one market report on 11 Nov had Brent up about 1.4% to roughly US$92.77. I could not confirm this against a second source.

Why it matters for Australia

Two things matter here. First, fuel: every unverified mine claim still moves the oil price, and Australia buys most of its refined fuel from Asian refiners that run on Gulf crude. Second, hosting risk. Rezaei's logic is that a base becomes a target if US aircraft use it against Iran. He named Europe, not Australia. But Australia hosts US bombers, tankers and joint facilities at Tindal, Darwin and Pine Gap, and has listed the IRGC as a state sponsor of terrorism. The Bessent move shows Washington takes Iran's reach seriously enough to relocate a cabinet member.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Abu Dhabi ends: prisoner swap agreed, nothing on territory; US envoys go to Putin today
item.description:
What happened

  • 11 Nov: Two days of Russia–Ukraine–US talks in Abu Dhabi ended. The sides agreed in principle to a large prisoner exchange. No numbers yet. Ukraine's Davyd Arakhamia said it could be "possibly even the largest overall". Russia's Vladimir Medinsky said details would come soon.
  • Territory did not move. Jared Kushner called it "the hardest" issue. Medinsky said "every inch of our land will be returned to Russia".
  • Security guarantees: Kushner reported "significant progress" and Ukraine's Rustem Umerov "huge progress". Neither gave details.
  • European security: Medinsky called it a central topic, with agreement on some points only. He said his team did not deal with the Europeans in Abu Dhabi.
  • Mood: Medinsky said the sides had "moved closer to peace". Arakhamia spoke of "good momentum" for a deal by the New Year.
  • 12 Nov: Kushner and Steve Witkoff are due to meet Putin in Moscow this morning (Moscow time). Putin aide Yuri Ushakov: "they're bringing something". Zelenskyy says he will meet the two envoys in Dublin the same day. Ushakov also says a Putin–Trump meeting at APEC is being worked on.
  • Zelenskyy asked Europe to name one representative for the talks by the end of November or at a Berlin meeting on 19 Nov.
  • 11 Nov: The CSTO summit in Moscow stripped Armenia of its voting rights, officially over unpaid dues. Armenia froze its participation in 2024.
  • 11 Nov: Russia's ambassador to the US, Alexander Darchiev, died aged 66. No cause was given.
  • The war goes on: Russia claimed 627 Ukrainian drones downed in one night (10–11 Nov) and says it took Voskresenka in Zaporizhzhia region. Reuters, via Meduza, says Ukrainian strikes have hit plants holding about 30% of Russia's refining capacity. Russia's battlefield claims are not independently verified.

Why it matters for Australia

The shape of the deal is the precedent. Prisoners are the easy part; territory and the European security order are the hard parts, and Europe still has no seat. Australia has backed Ukraine with more than A$1.5b and sanctions on Russia, so a settlement by New Year would raise quick questions about sanctions relief. The Armenia move is a smaller lesson in how Moscow treats a partner that drifts west. And a Putin–Trump meeting at APEC would happen in the same room as Albanese.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Rubio and Wang clear the path to Trump–Xi in Shenzhen; Albanese heads to APEC and Beijing
item.description:
What happened

  • 11 Nov: Secretary of State Rubio and Foreign Minister Wang Yi spoke by phone to prepare the Trump–Xi meeting at APEC in Shenzhen on 18–19 Nov. It would be their third face-to-face meeting this year. Xinhua quoted Wang calling the call "positive and constructive". There was no immediate US readout.
  • Rubio said on 10 Nov that work is under way on a three-way Trump–Xi–Putin meeting at APEC. Trump has said he would likely meet both to discuss ending the Iran war (per SCMP). SCMP also reports Iran pointing to a Chinese role in breaking its deadlock with Washington.
  • Australia: the PM's office said on 10 Nov that Albanese will go to COP31 in Antalya, then Manila for the ASEAN–Australia and East Asia summits, then APEC in Shenzhen, then Beijing for the Annual Leaders' Meeting with Premier Li. The release does not mention a Quad leaders' meeting in Manila, which Rubio has flagged.
  • Taiwan: Beijing still has not acknowledged the drills that Taiwan's defence minister described on 10 Nov as "area denial" training by the Liaoning group.
  • Japan: Xinhua and People's Daily are running hard on a report that a senior Japanese official wants nuclear weapons allowed into Japan in emergencies. I could not confirm the original remark independently. China's embassy also wants Tokyo to "severely punish" the Self-Defense Force officer who broke into it in March. Prosecutors have sought 18 months' jail; the verdict is due 24 Dec.

Why it matters for Australia

Albanese will be in Shenzhen while Trump and Xi meet, then sits down with Li in Beijing. That makes next week the main test of Australia's "stabilisation" policy this year. The risk is being squeezed: a warm Trump–Xi meeting lowers the cost to Beijing of pressing US allies, and Japan and the Philippines are already getting that treatment. If the Quad leaders do meet in Manila days before, Beijing will read Albanese's visit against it. A US–China–Russia conversation on Iran would also decide fuel-price questions for Australia in a room it is not in.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Where Australia puts its new air defences, and what the US midterms change for the alliance
item.description:
What happened

  • 11 Nov: ASPI's John Coyne argued that Australia's new integrated air and missile defences should mostly be based in the north. The government committed a further A$2.4b to Air 6500 (the joint air battle management system) in September. The Army's NASAMS short-range system became fully operational that month. A A$299.1m works proposal at RAAF Darwin would support the deployable air control unit.
  • Coyne's test is time: basing should follow how fast protection must be in place and how long it must last. He wants exercises that measure how long it takes to authorise, move, set up and sustain air defence units at Darwin, Tindal, Townsville and HMAS Stirling. Networks, he says, do not replace having interceptors where they are needed.
  • 11 Nov: Breaking Defense reported experts backing the Army's shift to littoral (coastal and island) operations. The Littoral Manoeuvre Group was set up in Brisbane in March. It will have three landing craft battalions, each with four medium and two heavy craft built by Austal. ANU's John Blaxland called it "a radical organisational design concept" but warned funding could slow it, with a budget review under way to pay for AUKUS submarines.
  • 11 Nov: ASPI's Fitriani and Justin Bassi argued the US midterms show "political alignments can change quickly but national interests endure". Democrats won both chambers on 3 Nov. They urge Canberra to lock cooperation into institutions: the Quad, the Australia–US–Japan–Philippines group, and an upgraded partnership with Manila.
  • 10 Nov: The US House voted 211–204 to send a resolution to impeach Defence Secretary Hegseth to committee. Republican Thomas Massie's eight articles include War Powers breaches over Iran and a US strike on an Iranian primary school. Breaking Defense says it is unlikely to advance before the new Congress sits in 2027.

Why it matters for Australia

These are the practical questions behind the strategy documents. Northern bases host US bombers, Marines and, from 2027, more submarine visits at Stirling. Iran's new threat to US bases in Europe is a reminder that hosting without air defence is a gamble. The littoral force is how the Army gets to the islands to Australia's north. Both compete with AUKUS for money. In Washington, a Democratic Congress from January and a wounded Pentagon chief mean more oversight and more uncertainty about US defence budgets, which AUKUS submarine production depends on.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Taiwan starts pulling its people out of PNG; US seabed mining auction nears off American Samoa
item.description:
What happened

  • 11 Nov: Taiwan's foreign ministry said it has begun withdrawing all diplomatic and technical staff from Papua New Guinea. A few will stay to wind up the office, which opened in 1990. PNG gave Representative Chiu Chen-yu and one other diplomat seven days to leave, and allowed one officer to stay up to a year to finish the closure.
  • About 100 Taiwanese live in PNG. Taiwan's missions in nearby countries will handle consular help.
  • Background: PNG ordered the office shut in July, citing its One-China policy. Taiwan confirmed the closure on 6 Nov, ended aid programs and stopped buying PNG LNG. Taiwan had taken about a third of PNG's LNG exports.
  • 19 Nov: The US plans to auction 31.5 million acres of deep-sea mining leases off American Samoa. A Devpolicy piece on 11 Nov warns of the risks for Pacific neighbours.
  • About 150 senior law enforcement officials met in Nouméa earlier this month on drug smuggling across the Pacific by sea, which RNZ quotes as "no longer a remote threat".
  • The Diplomat says Honiara has become a "staging ground for geopolitical competition" with little change for ordinary Solomon Islanders.

Why it matters for Australia

PNG is Australia's nearest neighbour and a treaty ally under the Pukpuk Treaty. The Taiwan exit is now physical, and the LNG loss is a real hole in Port Moresby's budget. Who fills it (Chinese buyers, or Australian support) will shape influence there. Applications for PNG citizens to join the ADF open on 16 Nov, so Canberra's offer is on show the same week. The US seabed auction puts Australia in an awkward spot: its main ally is pushing ahead with mining that many Pacific governments oppose, and Australia has just campaigned on its COP31 Pacific partnership.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: North Korea publishes its rewritten constitution; Kim pushes drones and military AI
item.description:
What happened

  • 10 Nov: North Korea's Naenara website posted the full text of the constitution as amended on 23 March. NK News says it confirms earlier reports: the country's territory is redefined and Kim Jong Un's powers are expanded. It closely matches a version leaked earlier by a Seoul National University professor. I could not read the exact wording, so treat the detail as second-hand.
  • It is the first time Pyongyang has shown the text since it pledged in early 2024 to rewrite the constitution, after Kim dropped peaceful unification as a goal.
  • 11 Nov: Kim Jong Un urged drone dominance and wider military use of AI, according to Indian broadcaster DD News. I could not check this against KCNA or Yonhap.
  • Also: Pyongyang has put its embassy building in Mexico up for sale for over US$2m (NK News). South Korea's foreign minister discussed North Korea with US and Ukrainian counterparts at the G7 meeting in Paris.

Why it matters for Australia

A constitution that defines territory and no longer treats the South as part of one nation turns border incidents into state-to-state disputes. That raises the stakes of events like the recent DMZ mine blast. Australia is a member of UN Command and helps enforce sanctions from Japan. The drone and AI push fits what North Korea is learning from Russia's war. Those lessons travel to other militaries in Australia's region. The embassy sale is a small sign of how short of cash the regime's diplomatic network is, and fits NK News reporting on its alleged cryptocurrency theft.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Iran claims three more tanker blasts in Hormuz, shows off a 'missile city' and denies any talks
item.description:
What happened

  • 10 Nov: The IRGC Navy said two "offending" tankers exploded on an "unauthorised" route south of the Strait of Hormuz. It then released footage of a third tanker that it says hit a naval mine. It accused the US military of luring tankers into the strait. These claims are unconfirmed: maritime agencies have not verified the IRGC's recent mine-strike announcements, though UKMTO did report two tankers hit or on fire on 7 Nov.
  • Iranian state TV says 11 tankers were attacked in 10 days. The IRGC denies the US claim that the mines have been cleared. A UKMTO weekly count to 10 Nov put transits about 65% below pre-war levels.
  • 10 Nov: The IRGC Aerospace Force unveiled a new underground missile base. Armed forces chief Maj. Gen. Abdollahi promised "surprises in the next war".
  • 10 Nov: Security chief Mohsen Rezaei posted that Washington should stop inventing "imaginary talks" and accept Iran's seven conditions. Per Al Jazeera, these include lifting the US blockade of Iran's southern ports and lifting sanctions. FM Araghchi denied any planned Rezaei–Vance meeting in Doha, which Turkey's intelligence chief had said Qatar would host next week.
  • The other track: Qatar's PM met Trump on 9 Nov and called the talks positive. Trump called the war "effectively over" militarily but said the blockade stays. The Jerusalem Post reports he gave Vance "a few days" to reach a deal. Rubio says a breakthrough is not imminent.
  • Spillover: Saudi Arabia confirmed a new attack on its East-West oil pipeline, the main bypass around Hormuz (reported via RT; the Houthis claimed it). Xinhua reported an ADNOC vessel damaged in UAE waters.
  • I could not confirm a fresh Brent price for 10 Nov. It was about US$94 at yesterday's brief.

Why it matters for Australia

This is the fuel story. Australia imports most of its refined fuel from Asian refiners that run on Gulf crude, so a strait running at a third of normal traffic keeps petrol, diesel and freight prices high here. The attack on the Saudi bypass pipeline matters because it is the main way around Hormuz. Albanese said on 7 Nov he has told Trump "publicly and directly" that it is time to de-escalate. A deal within Trump's "few days" would ease pressure fast; a collapse brings back Trump's threat to hit 38 bridges, and with it a new price spike.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Abu Dhabi day one: no breakthrough, and Moscow wants to talk about Europe before Ukraine
item.description:
What happened

  • 10 Nov: Russian, Ukrainian and US delegations met in Abu Dhabi for more than four hours. It was the first trilateral round since February. A second day is confirmed for 11 Nov and the Russian side has promised a press conference.
  • Who: Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff for the US; Rustem Umerov leads for Ukraine, with Kyrylo Budanov in the team; Vladimir Medinsky leads an 11-person Russian team including deputy foreign ministers Galuzin and Ryabkov. Meduza reports it also includes an FSB officer whom Ukraine accuses of trying to kill Budanov.
  • Topics, per ABC and Ukrainian media: security guarantees, territory, prisoners (a large exchange may be announced), reconstruction and a Europe-wide security framework.
  • The split on sequencing: a Russian delegation source told Reuters the Ukraine settlement is "just one aspect" of a wider European security discussion. Lavrov wants that framework agreed first and rejects a truce. Von der Leyen says wider talks come after a ceasefire.
  • Europe has no seat. EU, NATO, French, German and British officials are in Abu Dhabi and met the Ukrainians and Americans separately. Rubio says the aim is to widen the format to Europeans later.
  • Reported, not confirmed: The Economist says the US floated redrawing Donetsk and Luhansk borders so Russia could claim full control. A US official told Reuters each side might cede a little territory.
  • Reactions: Rubio called day one "very productive" with "a lot of work" left. Zelenskyy called it "constructive" but said "it's hard to deal with the Russians". Separately, RT reports the European Council decided to send EU military advisers to Ukraine.

Why it matters for Australia

Australia has given Ukraine more than A$1.5b in support and runs sanctions against Russia, so the terms of any deal matter here. The bigger issue is precedent. A settlement that rewards seizing territory, or lets great powers redesign a region's security order over the heads of the states in it, will be read closely in Beijing and across the Indo-Pacific. It also shows how Washington treats allies when it wants a deal: Europe is in the building but not in the room. And if a deal is close, expect pressure on partners like Australia over sanctions relief and reconstruction money.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: The Iran war reaches allied homelands: France blames the IRGC for the fridge hacks; US planes leave a second UK base
item.description:
What happened

  • 9–10 Nov: France formally blamed the IRGC for cyberattacks on 11–12 Oct that overheated fridges and freezers at about 700 supermarkets and other businesses. Some stores lost all fresh and frozen stock. A French intelligence report named the IRGC cyber unit Shahid Kaveh and three alleged members, working through fronts such as "CyberAveng3rs".
  • 10 Nov: France summoned Iran's ambassador. FM Barrot said "We rule nothing out". Paris will seek EU sanctions and arrest warrants.
  • ASPI notes similar incidents in the past week in Belgium, Luxembourg, Sweden, Finland, Ireland and Estonia. Who did those is less clear.
  • 9 Nov: At least 10 US KC-135 tankers left RAF Mildenhall and three Ospreys moved to RAF Lakenheath. Both bases went to FPCON Charlie, the second-highest alert. The Wall Street Journal says an Iranian threat prompted it; US officials have not described the threat. It follows the removal of US bombers from RAF Fairford in September.
  • UK PM Burnham says the bases are safe. MI5 says Iran-linked operations led to more than 50 arrests in a year.
  • Iran denies links to specific attacks in Britain, but the IRGC calls bases used by US forces legitimate targets.

Why it matters for Australia

Australia hosts US forces and joint facilities (Pine Gap, Darwin, Tindal, HMAS Stirling), so the UK experience is a preview of what hosting can cost in a US war. The fridge hacks hit everyday internet-connected equipment, not hardened networks. ASPI's point is that Australia's food, fuel, energy and port systems are linked in the same way: "The attacks have not hit Australia, but the country is not immune." ASD already advises operators to be able to isolate critical systems. Australia has also listed the IRGC as a state sponsor of terrorism, so it is not a neutral in Tehran's eyes.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Taiwan says the Liaoning group is running 'area denial' drills as Beijing courts Washington before APEC
item.description:
What happened

  • 10 Nov: Taiwan's defence minister Wellington Koo said China "has indeed conducted area denial drills in the Western Pacific", involving the Liaoning carrier group. China has declared no drills and its defence ministry did not comment. Last week Taiwan counted more than 100 Chinese navy and coast guard ships from the East China Sea to the Pacific.
  • At the same time Beijing is sending calm signals to Washington. On 9 Nov it extended its pause on measures against 11 US firms for two months. On 10 Nov the PLA handed over remains of US WWII airmen in Chengdu.
  • Trump and Xi are due to meet at APEC in Shenzhen on 18–19 Nov. SCMP expects few deliverables, with bigger items left for the G20 in Miami in December. Meduza, citing the WSJ, says the US, China and Russia cannot agree on a format for a three-way leaders' meeting.
  • The Nvidia affair hangs over it. The ABC reports CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset. Congress is pressing for tighter chip curbs. RT reports Trump is backing Huang despite an FBI probe.
  • Pressure on US allies continues: Global Times ran pieces against Japan and the Philippines, and China's coast guard patrolled around the Senkakus on 9 Nov.
  • Next week: ASEAN summit in Manila (16–18 Nov). Lowy says Washington has signalled a Quad leaders' meeting on the sidelines, the first in more than two years.

Why it matters for Australia

Area denial drills east of Taiwan rehearse keeping US and allied forces, which could include Australian ones, out of a Taiwan fight. That is the scenario AUKUS submarines and northern base upgrades are meant for. The pattern also matters: Beijing is easing off Washington while leaning on Tokyo and Manila, Australia's two closest regional defence partners. A Trump–Xi meeting with a friendly tone and little content could leave allies carrying the pressure. The Quad meeting in Manila is where Albanese can test how much the US still backs the grouping.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: PNG pays for dropping Taiwan as Australia opens ADF recruiting there; AUKUS critics and defenders trade blows
item.description:
What happened

  • Taiwan confirmed it will close its Port Moresby office (open since 1990), pull all staff and end all aid and technical programs. PNG ordered the mission shut in July, citing its One-China policy. Beijing welcomed that.
  • Taiwan has also stopped buying PNG LNG and will sign no new spot contracts. RNZ says Taiwan took roughly a third of PNG's LNG exports. Taipei says the move will have "a substantial impact" on PNG's export earnings, and blames Chinese "political pressure and economic influence". RNZ gives no independent evidence of that pressure.
  • Applications open on 16 Nov for 100 PNG students and graduates aged 18–25 to join the ADF, under the 2025 Pukpuk Treaty. The pilot costs A$65m and the first cohort is due to be sworn in by late 2027. An ASPI piece warns that with thousands likely to be rejected, selection must be openly scored or it "will look corrupt".
  • AUKUS: the privately run AUKUS Public Inquiry (chaired by former ADF chief Chris Barrie and Peter Garrett) reported on 4 Nov, calling AUKUS "the worst, riskiest and most costly defence decision ever". On 10 Nov a US Studies Centre fellow replied in ASPI's Strategist that the verdict "lacks credibility" because it plays down China's coercion, while accepting that delivery timelines and nuclear waste are real concerns.
  • Also: a no-confidence motion against Vanuatu PM Jotham Napat was withdrawn on 9 Nov.

Why it matters for Australia

PNG is Australia's nearest neighbour and now a treaty ally. Losing a buyer for a third of its LNG hurts Port Moresby's budget, and Canberra is its lender of last resort. If Chinese buyers or finance fill the gap, Beijing's leverage grows in the one Pacific state Australia has bound itself to defend. The ADF recruitment pilot is a test of whether the Pukpuk Treaty delivers something ordinary Papua New Guineans can see and trust. The AUKUS exchange shows the home debate hardening into two camps that disagree on the basic question: how big is the China threat?

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: North Korea tests a 'high-speed torpedo' for 2027 service; Kim Yo Jong rebuffs the UN chief
item.description:
What happened

  • 9 Nov: North Korea tested what KCNA calls a "new-type high-speed torpedo weapon system", fired in the East Sea (Sea of Japan). KCNA reported it on 10 Nov and said the navy will be equipped with it from the start of 2027.
  • It is the second public test in a month. After the first, on 15 Oct, KCNA claimed AI guidance, and some analysts suggested a supercavitating design. This time KCNA gave fewer details and no photos. The claims are not independently verified.
  • It follows a mid-October test of two types of submarine-launched cruise missile.
  • 10 Nov: Kim Yo Jong rejected UN Secretary-General Guterres's call for the two Koreas to reopen military hotlines after a mine blast in the DMZ. She said he would bear responsibility for any incident caused by the South.
  • Summit watch: Yonhap and NK News report experts saying a Democratic House cannot stop a Trump–Kim summit but could limit what Trump offers. Pyongyang's apparent demand to be recognised as a nuclear power remains the obstacle.

Why it matters for Australia

A fast torpedo, sub-launched cruise missiles and a new destroyer class all point the same way: North Korea is building a navy that can threaten ships, not just a missile force. Australian ships and aircraft regularly help enforce UN sanctions on North Korea from Japan, in those waters. Australia is also a member of UN Command, so a border incident with hotlines cut is a direct interest. Any Trump–Kim deal that accepts North Korea's nuclear status would weaken the non-proliferation rules Australia relies on.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Qatar takes Iran's two-day Hormuz plan to Trump; no breakthrough yet
item.description:
What happened

  • 9 Nov (US time): Trump met Qatari PM Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani at the White House for just under an hour, behind closed doors. There was no public readout. Axios reported Qatar wanted Trump to give diplomacy more time.
  • The proposal Qatar carried, as reported: Iran reopens Hormuz and stops attacks on Gulf tankers. In return the US lifts its naval and economic blockade and releases about US$8b of Iranian funds held in Qatar. Iran has cut its proposed implementation period from seven days to two, which spokesman Baqaei called a "sign of goodwill".
  • Trump on 60 Minutes, asked about escalating: "I'm not looking to. I don't think there's any reason to." He said Task Force Iron Gate, which extends the blockade to land routes, "is in full force and effect". Rubio said the sides are not "at the verge of a breakthrough" and called Iran's demands "unacceptable".
  • Iran's terms: Baqaei says there is "no reason" to send its 60% enriched uranium abroad. He says any deal must include lifting sanctions, ending the blockade, unfreezing assets and a ceasefire on all fronts. Iranian media cite a security source saying there will be no talks until the US acts on seven conditions (unconfirmed).
  • At sea: the UK's maritime agency (UKMTO) reclassified Saturday's tanker fire north of Khasab, Oman, as an attack. Iranian state TV said four tankers were "brought to a standstill" in 24 hours. Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline was hit again, causing a "limited fire" in Medina region.
  • Brent fell about 4.7% on 9 Nov to roughly US$93.75 (session low US$92.80). It had already dropped 16% the week before.

Why it matters for Australia

Australia imports most of its liquid fuel as refined product from Asian refineries that run on Gulf crude. A deal that reopens Hormuz would be the single biggest relief for petrol and diesel prices and for the RBA's inflation outlook. Equally, a breakdown would push prices back toward US$100. The Quad foreign ministers (31 Oct) listed Hormuz freedom of navigation as a shared priority, so Canberra is on record. Any mine-clearance or escort coalition after a deal could bring requests for ADF contributions.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Russia, Ukraine and US resume peace talks in Abu Dhabi
item.description:
What happened

  • 10–11 Nov: US-mediated trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi, the first since the process stalled when the Iran war began in late February.
  • Delegations: Witkoff and Kushner for the US. Ukraine sends Rustem Umerov with Kyrylo Budanov, Sergiy Kyslytsya and Davyd Arakhamia. Russia's reinforced team is led by Vladimir Medinsky and reportedly includes Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin.
  • Agenda: post-war security arrangements, de-escalation and humanitarian issues. Kushner says a "comprehensive and lasting settlement" needs Russia and Europe to deal directly on security.
  • An EU team led by Bjoern Seibert (von der Leyen's chief of staff) is attending, with E3 national security advisers, Italy and a NATO representative. Russia has not said whether it will meet them.
  • Both sides kept striking energy targets on the eve of the talks. Zelensky says Russia used North Korean-made KN-23 missiles on a key energy facility on Saturday (preliminary findings, site unnamed).
  • Trump has said Ukraine may end up taking "a little bit different shape" (via RT, unconfirmed wording).

Why it matters for Australia

Australia's support package for Ukraine and its sanctions on Russia are tied to how this settlement handles territory. A deal that rewards seizing land by force cuts against the rules-based order Canberra argues for in the Indo-Pacific. There is also a direct consular angle. ABC reports Daryl Fladung, 38, a Queensland security guard with no military experience, flew to Moscow in April and signed a Russian army contract. He has been missing since late June and is feared dead. He is the first Australian known to have joined Russia's army since 2022. DFAT would not confirm what it knows.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Iran announces offensive doctrine with 'no geographical limits'
item.description:
What happened

  • 9 Nov: Army spokesman Brig. Gen. Mohammad Akraminia said Iran's military doctrine has moved from a defensive to an offensive approach. "Effective response" without geographical limits is now operational strategy (ISNA, via ANI). IRNA ties this to new directives from Commander-in-Chief Mojtaba Khamenei.
  • The same day, President Pezeshkian said the Supreme Leader had ordered officials to end the state of "neither war nor peace". He added: "We favor dialogue and negotiations... we will not surrender to force and bullying."
  • Press TV ran an opinion piece listing possible targets: US bases across the Gulf, Jordan and Djibouti, plus Diego Garcia, undersea internet cables, energy terminals, Gulf desalination plants and Israeli nuclear and tech sites.
  • No source formally links the doctrine announcement to Pezeshkian's remarks. The link is implied by timing.

Why it matters for Australia

Naming Diego Garcia, and asserting that any territory that "facilitates attacks" on Iran is a target, is deterrence messaging aimed at US partners. Australia hosts US force posture and has ADF personnel in the Middle East. The threat to subsea cables on Asia–Europe routes matters to Australia's data links. Threats to Gulf energy and desalination plants feed straight into fuel prices.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Trump heads for APEC in Shenzhen and floats a Trump–Xi–Putin meeting
item.description:
What happened

  • Trump says he expects to meet Putin and Xi together during his trip to the APEC leaders' meeting in Shenzhen on 18–19 Nov: "one of the meetings I think will be with President Putin and President Xi". He says the agenda includes "denuclearization" and ending the Iran war. Peskov says "work is underway". Beijing has announced no trilateral.
  • A Manila stop on 16 Nov has been reported (New York Post, citing the Philippine palace). This is not confirmed by the White House.
  • SCMP reports US military transport aircraft landing in Shenzhen, widely read as preparation for the visit.
  • 10 Nov: China's Commerce Ministry extended for two more months its suspension of export-control measures against 16 US entities (listed April 2025). It said this implements the consensus from the "eighth round" of US–China trade talks. The broader trade truce runs to January.
  • This would be the third Trump–Xi meeting this year, after Beijing in May and Washington in September.

Why it matters for Australia

A great-power deal over Iran or Ukraine struck in China, without allies present, is the 'Yalta 2.0' scenario Lowy's Interpreter warns about. Canberra would want assurance that Taiwan, the South China Sea and the alliance are not part of any trade-off. A stable US–China trade truce helps Australian exporters. A summit that reads as Washington accommodating Beijing would sharpen the domestic AUKUS debate. ASPI this week stressed that the PLA Southern Theater Command, not global Chinese dominance, is Australia's most direct military threat.

item.title: Chinese consulate presses Victoria over killing of delivery rider in Melbourne
item.description:
What happened

  • 6 Nov, about 8.10pm: a Chinese national working as a HungryPanda food-delivery rider was killed near Queen Victoria Market, Melbourne. Another rider was injured. Police say two riders confronted a man suspected of tampering with their bikes, and an altercation followed. A 51-year-old man was arrested.
  • The Chinese Consulate-General activated its "emergency consular protection mechanism". Consul-General Fang Xinwen phoned the Victorian Premier and asked that the perpetrator be "severely punished". Global Times reports the Premier promised justice.
  • A Weibo hashtag about the victim's long working hours drew more than 4.9 million views. SCMP reports online outrage in China over delivery-rider safety.

Why it matters for Australia

The case is now a bilateral consular issue as well as a criminal one. Beijing's public pressure on a state premier tests how Canberra and Victoria handle Chinese official advocacy while police and courts work independently. It also shapes perceptions of Australia among Chinese students, workers and tourists, a key relationship since stabilisation. Watch whether Beijing's framing stays on this one case or widens into claims about the safety of Chinese nationals in Australia.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Iran: Trump meets Qatar's mediator as Tehran says the next move is Washington's
item.description:
What happened

  • 9 Nov (US time): Trump meets Qatari PM Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani at the White House at noon Eastern (about 4am Tuesday AEDT). Vance is also due to meet him separately. Qatar denies reports that the US–Iran talks have failed.
  • Araghchi says Qatar-mediated talks produced a "two-day plan": the US takes agreed steps on day one and Iran reopens Hormuz on day two. Qatar's mediation cut it down from an earlier seven-day plan. Tehran wants sanctions relief and fewer US troops in the region. Araghchi's line is that it is now the White House's turn to choose.
  • Trump told CNN that new large-scale strikes are "highly unlikely" if talks progress, but he has three carriers in the region. He told CBS: "We would have had a deal except for this election." Rubio says the talks are "not productive" and Iran's demands are "simply unacceptable".
  • Xinhua, citing Axios, reports Vance has been in near-daily indirect contact with Tehran for two weeks through Qatar and Pakistan, and has proposed direct talks. Progress is described as very slow.
  • 5 Nov: Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei met Putin in the Kremlin and handed over a letter from Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. Russia's military intelligence chief Igor Kostyukov also attended. Rezaei said Iran won't negotiate on ending the war or reopening Hormuz until the US meets seven conditions.
  • Also reported: a suspected Iranian drone attack halted Iraq's Khor Mor gas field (attribution unconfirmed). Iran's navy reports another tanker fire after a mine strike east of Hormuz.

Why it matters for Australia

Fuel is the most direct link. Australia imports almost all its liquid fuel as refined product from Asian refineries that depend on Gulf crude. Oil prices swung on Monday on Trump's and Rubio's mixed messages. A deal would ease pressure on prices and on the RBA. Failed talks plus three carriers could mean renewed strikes on power plants and bridges. Canberra has publicly urged de-escalation. Marles has tied any ADF role in Hormuz to a lasting ceasefire. The Qatar meeting is the clearest sign yet of whether that condition is getting closer.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Saudi–Houthi war escalates: village strike near Sanaa, missiles at Riyadh
item.description:
What happened

  • 7 Nov: Airstrikes hit al-Shariya village in Bani Hushaysh, a Houthi stronghold east of Sanaa. Houthi-run Saba says at least 33 people were killed and 39 wounded, mostly women and children. Reuters could not verify the figures. Saudi Arabia's Center for International Communication says it is investigating the reports.
  • 8 Nov: The Saudi-led coalition says it intercepted a Houthi ballistic missile aimed at the Eastern Province and two missiles fired at Riyadh. Falling debris damaged an administrative building in Riyadh's Aramco Tower. The Energy Ministry reported limited damage and no casualties. The Houthis also claim attacks on Saudi airports and Aramco storage sites.
  • The fighting resumed in July and ended the 2022 UN-brokered truce. The IOM says more than 200,000 people have been displaced since then.

Why it matters for Australia

With Hormuz effectively shut, Saudi exports that bypass the strait (the East-West pipeline to Red Sea ports) matter more to the Asian refineries that supply Australia's fuel. Houthi strikes on Saudi energy sites and a Houthi naval blockade declared against Saudi Arabia threaten that bypass. A wider Gulf war also makes the region harder to stabilise even if a US–Iran deal is reached. That affects any future ADF maritime contribution.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Russia pounds Ukraine's grid, reportedly with North Korean missiles, before Abu Dhabi talks
item.description:
What happened

  • 7–8 Nov: Russian strikes cut power to more than 600,000 people in Dnipropetrovsk region (DTEK) and about 250,000 in Kharkiv region. The Energy Ministry says the 7 Nov attack hit five regions and disrupted transmission to Kyiv.
  • 9 Nov: Zelensky says preliminary findings show Russia used North Korean KN-23 ballistic missiles on a key energy facility. This is the first time he has named the model in this campaign. He asked allies for more interceptors and tougher sanctions.
  • Russia's MoD says it will keep striking fuel and energy facilities it says support Ukraine's military. It claims 430 Ukrainian drones were downed overnight. DPR head Pushilin claims advances along the Donetsk front near Druzhkovka (unverified).
  • US-brokered US–Russia–Ukraine talks are due in Abu Dhabi on 10–11 Nov, with Witkoff and Kushner leading for the US.
  • Deputy FM Pankin told TASS that a US–Russia "diesel deal" shows "opportunities remain" to restore business ties. He called it a temporary exemption, not sanctions relief. Merz says he wouldn't rule out meeting Putin at the Miami G20.

Why it matters for Australia

KN-23s used against Ukraine show Indo-Pacific and European security are linked. Combat use helps Pyongyang refine missiles that threaten Japan and South Korea. Australia has sanctioned Russia and given military aid to Ukraine. If Washington offers Moscow sanctions exemptions, Canberra will have to decide whether its own autonomous sanctions follow.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: China's DF-61 ICBM moves fast into routine training
item.description:
What happened

  • 5 Nov: CCTV reported that the DF-61 road-mobile ICBM, first shown at the September 2025 parade, is in routine PLA Rocket Force training. The training covers field mobility, moving between launch positions and launch procedures. The report marked 66 years since the DF-1 launch. State media also showed the rarely seen DF-100 cruise missile.
  • CCTV gave no range, numbers or basing. Training does not prove full operational readiness.
  • Social media claims of an inland ICBM test, possibly including a mid-course interception, are unconfirmed (SCMP).
  • SCMP analysts also ask whether recent PLA Navy deployments in the western Pacific and South China Sea rehearse keeping US forces out of a Taiwan conflict.
  • Background: In September 2024 China fired a DF-31B ICBM into the South Pacific. Reports say it fired a submarine-launched missile into the Pacific in July 2026. The US and allies want 24 hours' notice of such launches.

Why it matters for Australia

China's fast nuclear build-up underpins its effort to deter the US from intervening over Taiwan, the scenario that would test the alliance and AUKUS. Australia is within ICBM range, and recent PLA tests have landed in the South Pacific near Pacific partners. ASPI argues the PLA Southern Theater Command matters most to Australia. A larger strategic nuclear force covers its conventional operations closer to home.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: North Korea tests new missiles and wins new embassies as its missiles appear in Ukraine
item.description:
What happened

  • 5 Nov: KCNA said the Missile Administration test-fired a new surface-to-air missile system, overseen by Gen. Kim Jong Sik. Separately, a strategic cruise missile unit hit a simulated airport target. This followed a reported cluster-type cruise missile warhead test on 2 Nov. The performance claims are not independently confirmed.
  • Belarus has opened an embassy in Pyongyang, and Brazil's first ambassador in a decade has taken up his post (NK News).
  • North Korean loudspeakers are visible at the border again, but no broadcasts have been heard.
  • 9 Nov: Zelensky says Russia used KN-23s on Ukraine's grid (see Europe story).
  • Australia's latest move is not new: on 22 Oct it sanctioned Yu Pu Ung, Sim Hyon Sop and two IT firms over fake remote-work schemes that fund weapons programs. The US has since blacklisted a Seychelles-based crypto exchange over North Korean money laundering.

Why it matters for Australia

Pyongyang is testing air defences and strikes on airfields, the kind of targets that matter to US bases in Japan and South Korea. Australia relies on those bases in a regional crisis. North Korean IT workers have used stolen Australian identity documents to win remote jobs, so the cyber and sanctions threat reaches Australian firms directly. More embassies in Pyongyang mean its isolation is easing.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: PLA mass far-seas deployment around Taiwan, with no exercise name
item.description:
What happened

Taiwan's NSC chief Joseph Wu reported more than 100 PLA Navy and China Coast Guard vessels in the Western Pacific on 3 Nov. On 2 Nov there were 49 air sorties, the highest single day this year. AEI/ISW analysts count four task groups from the Eastern, Northern and Southern Theatre Commands between Taiwan and Guam. These include the Liaoning group, and the Fujian left Sanya on 2 Nov. Daily counts have dropped back since (4 aircraft, 6 vessels in the 24 hours to 6am on 8 Nov).

Why it matters for Australia

This drill practises keeping outside navies out of the area, which is the job the US alliance and AUKUS force posture would face in a crisis. It also comes ahead of APEC in Shenzhen (18–19 Nov), where Albanese may go on to Beijing (SCMP, unconfirmed). A visit would test how Canberra keeps stabilisation with China going while this is underway.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Hormuz still closed as mines hit tankers and Qatar mediates
item.description:
What happened

Iran says two tankers caught fire after hitting mines on an "unauthorised route." Explosions were heard on Qeshm Island and at Jask, days after US strikes. CENTCOM disabled a St Kitts-flagged ship in the Gulf of Oman. Trump called Friday's strikes on Iranian air defences "minor" and is weighing a larger wave now that the midterms are over. The IRGC lifted its self-imposed 2,000 km ballistic missile range cap. Iran is reviewing Qatari proposals on its nuclear program.

Why it matters for Australia

Australia imports most of its liquid fuel, so a long closure hits the economy directly. The RBA's 25-point hike to 4.85% cited war-driven energy costs. The ADF has given defensive support to Gulf states since March, so any escalation after the midterms raises the question of how far that commitment goes.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Abu Dhabi talks set for 10–11 Nov after Trump meets Putin's envoy
item.description:
What happened

Trump met Kirill Dmitriev at the White House and said a deal may be close, but gave no details and didn't meet the Ukrainian delegation. Witkoff says working-level talks between Russia, the US and Ukraine will cover post-war security arrangements, de-escalation and humanitarian issues. A Kremlin aide says sanctions relief for Russia's sovereign wealth fund is being discussed. The EU's Kallas rejects any deal made without Europe.

Why it matters for Australia

Australia has sanctions on Russia and has sent Bushmasters to Ukraine. A deal that rewards taking territory by force and lifts sanctions sets a precedent that would be read closely in the Indo-Pacific. Australia would also have to decide whether to keep its own sanctions if Washington drops its.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: North Korea's fourth weapons launch in a month
item.description:
What happened

KCNA reported cluster-bomb warhead tests (1 Nov), a strategic cruise missile with a dispersal warhead (2 Nov), and a new air-defence missile plus a cruise missile strike drill (4 Nov). NK News says the drill photos were heavily doctored. Talks with Washington remain in doubt.

Why it matters for Australia

The ADF regularly sends aircraft and ships to monitor UN sanctions on North Korea. Australia is also strengthening ties with Japan and South Korea. Cluster and dispersal warheads point to battlefield use against airfields, which also matters for how Australia thinks about protecting its own bases.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: The Pacific contest: Solomons treaty, PNG explosive, Quad in Atlanta
item.description:
What happened

  • Canberra and Honiara have an in-principle treaty, reportedly with A$980m in extra funding. Solomon Islands keeps its security pact with China, and PM Wale faces a no-confidence motion.
  • The ABC says a Chinese military-grade explosive found in a container in PNG is a real weapon. Chinese officials had called it a wine bottle.
  • Quad foreign ministers (31 Oct, Atlanta) raised concerns about economic coercion and export restrictions, and announced critical minerals work and port cooperation in Fiji. A leaders' summit is planned for Manila this month.
  • The ADF sent a C-130, a Citation and 20 personnel to help fight the East Kalimantan fires.

Why it matters for Australia

Pacific security partnerships are where Australia competes most directly with China for influence, and where Canberra has the most to lose if partners hedge.
